The relative age effect (RAE) — the overrepresentation of players born early in the selection year — is one of the most robust findings in sports science, yet how much it varies across countries and over time remains surprisingly underexplored. Drawing on birth-date data for 49,578 male professional footballers across 44 national systems and five birth cohorts (1985–2009), this study describes three patterns that have not previously been examined together. RAE magnitude varies enormously across national football systems, ranging from close to zero to birth-quarter gaps exceeding 40 percentage points. It has also increased across successive birth cohorts: players born in 2005–2009 show birth-quarter imbalances roughly 9 percentage points wider than those born in 1985–1989. Common macro-level indicators — national footballing strength, gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, and population — show at most weak and inconsistent associations with cross-national differences in RAE and do not account for the historical increase once country and cohort are held fixed. Together, these findings provide a comparative benchmark for understanding cross-national and historical variation in relative age effects.

Elite footballers are disproportionately born early in the selection year. Since Barnsley, Thompson, and Barnsley’s discovery of this pattern in junior ice hockey [ 1 ], relative age effects (RAEs) have been documented across dozens of sports and national contexts, including football [ 2 ], ice hockey, and basketball, and confirmed by successive meta-analyses [ 3 , 4 ]. Within any nominally same-aged cohort, relatively older children may enjoy physical, cognitive, and behavioural advantages over their younger peers [ 5 , 6 ]. These initial differences are not, however, the whole of the phenomenon. They can be amplified through selection and through the secondary benefits that follow it: players identified as more promising may receive better coaching, more playing opportunities, stronger competition, and other developmental advantages that accumulate over time, and there is good reason to treat relative age and biological maturity as distinct rather than interchangeable constructs [ 7 ]. Among adult professional footballers, players born in the first quarter of the selection year typically outnumber those born in the fourth quarter by ratios exceeding two to one [ 8 , 9 ].

The resulting literature has concentrated primarily on establishing that RAEs exist and on identifying the mechanisms — maturational advantage, coach bias, dropout among late-born players — that plausibly sustain them at the individual level [ 3 , 10 ]. This work has also examined how RAE magnitude varies with moderators such as competition level and talent-identification intensity [ 11 , 12 ].

Football provides an especially informative setting for these questions because it combines highly standardised age-group selection with substantial institutional variation across countries. Existing theories implicitly treat RAE as a near-universal consequence of grouping children by birth date within a selection year, with variation across settings read as secondary noise around a common phenomenon. Two questions that follow directly from that assumption remain underexplored: how much RAE actually differs between national football systems, and whether it has changed across historical time. Existing studies typically examine a single country or a small set of countries at a single point in time, and large-scale comparative evidence remains scarce [ 8 , 13 – 15 ]. A sufficiently large and comparable dataset can answer both questions directly, without first having to decide between competing explanations for why RAE occurs at all.

This study provides one of the largest comparative analyses of professional footballers to examine cross-national and historical variation in RAE simultaneously.
